question: According to a UNESCO report published on the occasion of the 2026 International Holocaust Remembrance Day, more than three quarters of teachers surveyed in the EU had encountered antisemitic incidents in their classroom. The survey collected responses from over 2 000 teachers across 23 Member States. It shows alarmingly high levels of Holocaust denial and physical violence against Jewish students.

70 % of teachers also reported that they had received no professional training on how to recognise and address antisemitism. This report was published with the support of the Commission. In the light of this: 1.

How does the Commission plan to counter this alarming trend and what steps will it take to ensure that the safety of Jewish students and the accurate teaching of the Holocaust are treated as a priority across the EU, while respecting subsidiarity?

Which special EU funding instruments (e.g. Erasmus+, the Citizens, Equality, Rights & Values programme) have been used to combat antisemitism and how does the Commission verify that these funds are used effectively for this purpose?
Is the Commission willing to reallocate budget, staff and resources to EU efforts to counter antisemitism, including to the EU Coordinator on combating antisemitism and fostering Jewish life?
answer: According to the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, Member States are fully responsible for the organisation of their education systems and for the content of teaching.

The Commission is supporting curricula developers and educators by providing dedicated resources, including through financing the project ‘addressing antisemitism through education’ implemented by the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation (Unesco) (1).

The EU Strategy on Combating Antisemitism and Fostering Jewish Life (2021-2030) (2) invites schools across the EU to ensure that all pupils learn about Jewish life in Europe, the Holocaust and antisemitism and mark the annual International Holocaust Remembrance Day. The Commission will develop an EU citizenship competence framework to strengthen curricular development in this area.

The fight against antisemitism is funded under various funding programmes, for example the Citizens, Equality, Rights and Values programme, Creative Europe, the Erasmus+, the Neighbourhood, Development and International Cooperation Instrument — Global Europe, the Internal Security Fund and the Horizon Europe Framework Programme for Research and Innovation.

Project applications are examined and approved in compliance with the applicable eligibility rules. If there is evidence of a beneficiary acting in violation of applicable legislation, EU values, applicable EU acquis and international law, in the implementation of a project, the Commission and Member States consider the available means to terminate the cooperation and recover the EU funds.

Based on a College decision of December 2019, the Coordinator on Combating Antisemitism and Fostering Jewish Life, together with three staff members, currently leads the implementation of the EU Strategy on Combating Antisemitism and Fostering Jewish Life (2021-2030).
As part of mainstreaming the fight against antisemitism, an array of colleagues in many other Commission services contribute to the implementation of the strategy through relevant actions.
Strategies to counter antisemitism: a handbook for educators, Unesco, 2025: https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000396116. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:52021DC0615.
